what_its_for: Trabectedin is a cancer medicine (chemotherapy) used to treat a type of soft tissue cancer called liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma that has spread or cannot be removed by surgery. It works by blocking the growth of cancer cells and helping to slow or stop the cancer from spreading.
how_to_take: Trabectedin is NOT a pill you take by mouth. It is given as a slow drip (infusion) into your vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor at a hospital or infusion center. Each treatment takes about 24 hours to complete. You will also be given other medicines before your infusion, including a steroid called dexamethasone, to help protect your liver and reduce side effects like nausea.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate the right dose for you based on your height and weight (called body surface area). Most adults receive one infusion every 3 weeks (one treatment cycle). Your doctor may adjust your dose or delay your treatment depending on how your body responds and any side effects you experience. Never try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because trabectedin is given by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital, a missed dose is rare. However, if you miss or need to reschedule your appointment, call your doctor or treatment center as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your doctor will decide the best time to give your next treatment.
storage: Trabectedin is stored and prepared by pharmacy staff at the hospital or infusion center. You do not need to store this medicine at home. The prepared infusion must be used within a certain time frame and kept at controlled room temperature (not above 86°F / 30°C) by your healthcare team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol during treatment, as it can increase the risk of liver damage. Do not take any new medicines, vitamins, herbal supplements, or over-the-counter drugs without first talking to your doctor or pharmacist, as some medicines can interact with trabectedin. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they may affect how this drug works in your body. Avoid crowded places or people who are sick, since this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections. Use effective birth control during treatment and for several months after your last dose, as trabectedin can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this could be a sign of infection); unusual bruising or bleeding; severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark brown or cola-colored urine (possible muscle breakdown); yellowing of your skin or eyes, or severe stomach pain (possible liver problems); severe nausea, vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down; shortness of breath or chest pain; swelling, redness, or pain at the infusion site; or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Trabectedin does not cure cancer, but it is designed to slow the growth and spread of cancer. Your doctor will check how well the treatment is working through regular scans and blood tests. It may take several treatment cycles before your doctor can tell if the medicine is helping. Every patient responds differently, so be patient and keep all your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Trabectedin can seriously harm an unborn baby. Do not become pregnant during treatment or for at least 2 months after your last dose if you are a woman, or 5 months if your partner received treatment. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 3 months after your last dose. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted or treatment may not be appropriate. Children: The safety and effectiveness of trabectedin in children has not been established. Older adults (65 and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects; your doctor will monitor you closely. Always tell your full medical team about all your health conditions and medicines.
